To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the average household income increased by $1,200 (in real 1999 dollars) in the 1990’s.

• During the 199os, productivity improvements and price reductions in Australian infrastructure services raised average household incomes in all jurisdictions and in every deciles of the income distribution; • The main sources of change were productivity improvements and price declines in the electricity and communications industries; • The main effects were price effects (direct and indirect) and income effects; • The direct price effects were real price declines in most infrastructure services; • The indirect price effects were lower infrastructure costs for industry, which led to lower prices

• The distributional impacts of the changes in Australian infrastructure industries during the 1990’s were small, slightly favour ing more affluent households, and were dominated by the impacts of changes in the telecommunications and electricity industries.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the distributional effects of infrastructure industries in Australia.
the distributional effects of changes in the prices, costs, and incomes associated with infrastructure services in the 1990-99 period.

the effects of changes in infrastructure industries during the 1990’s on the income distribution of households in Australia; and the distributional effects of changes in the Australian economy during the 1995 to 2000 period, which were caused by changes in the infrastructure industries.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the reforms and other developments in Australian infrastructure services during the 1990’s have improved the distribution of incomes.
the distributional effects were small, slightly favour in favour of more affluent households.

the distributional effects of the reforms and other developments in Australian infrastructure industries during the 1990's were small, slightly favourable to higher income households, but with some significant exceptions.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the distributional effects of the changes were small.
, on the whole, the distributional effects of changes to the Australian infrastructure industries during the 1990's have been relatively small.
the changes in Australian infrastructure industries in the 1990's have been broadly positive for all households.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the distributional impacts of infrastructure are complex and can vary significantly between jurisdictions.
the distributional effects of the changes were modest and slightly favourable to higher income groups.
the distributional effects of changes in Australian infrastructure industries are likely to be small and, on average, slightly favour more affluent households.
